Tokens-per-Parameter Coverage Is Critical for Robust LLM Scaling Law Extrapolation

Joshua Shay Kricheli    Alexander Lawrence Reid    Venkata Gandikota & Paulo Shakarian Affiliation: Syracuse University Email: {jkrichel,areid04,vsgandik,pashakar}@syr.edu    Soumajyoti Sarkar ††thanks: This work does not relate to the author’s position at Amazon. Affiliation: Amazon AGI Foundations
Abstract

Neural scaling laws approximate a language model’s loss as a power-law function of parameter count NN and token count DD. Following Chinchilla-style compute-optimal training, many studies fit scaling laws from runs performed under a fixed tokens-per-parameter (TPP) ratio kk and set D=k​ND=kN. We show that this collinear design, combined with the empirically common near-equality of the exponents governing NN and DD, induces an inherent ill-conditioning in the Gauss-Newton least-squares problem: the condition number of the design grows as the inverse square of the gap between the NN and DD-exponents. The scale coefficients become practically unidentifiable, with confidence intervals inflating by an order of magnitude or more, yielding a “sloppy” model whose extrapolations degrade sharply off the training ray. We prove this for four scaling-law formalisms and derive a closed-form TPP-diversity threshold that is necessary and sufficient for well-conditioned estimation. Empirically, non-collinear designs outperform collinear ones on held-out splits with a 97.3%97.3\% win rate across four laws, five corpora, multiple floating point precision modes. We further show the degeneracy is rooted in Jacobian geometry and is not an artifact of the loss function: any smooth estimation objective whose curvature involves the Jacobian inherits the same ill-conditioning.

1 Introduction

Scaling laws have become a cornerstone of large language model (LLM) research, providing a predictive framework for estimating model performance as a function of compute, dataset size, and parameter count (hestness2017deep; rosenfeld2019constructive; kaplan2020scaling; alabdulmohsin2022revisiting; caballero2023broken; bahri2024explaining). The seminal Chinchilla study (hoffmann2022training) proposed that model size NN and training tokens DD scale linearly under a fixed compute budget with D≈20​ND\approx 20N. A recent survey of 50+ studies finds the fitted law shifts substantially under changes to the included D/ND/N range, with the optimal ratio a recurring source of disagreement (li2025misfitting). These works established the fixed TPP (Tokens-per-Parameter) heuristic in the compute-optimal setting. This ratio is a prescription for how to allocate compute when training a single model, not a design for the experimental grid from which scaling laws are derived. Yet fixed-TPP grids are widely used for exactly this purpose. Cerebras-GPT (dey2023cerebrasgptopencomputeoptimallanguage) trains 111M-13B models at D=20​ND=20N; gadre2024language parameterize over-trained scaling along constant-MM lines where each slice is itself collinear; the OLMo ladder fits Chinchilla at fixed Chinchilla multiples (bhagia2025establishingtaskscalinglaws); and DataDecide reports that eight scaling-law variants fitted at D=100​ND=100N fail to beat a naïve single-scale baseline (magnusson2025datadecidepredictbestpretraining). The practical stakes are high: choshen2024hitchhiker fit over 1,0001{,}000 laws to 485485 published models and find estimates sensitive to the choice and coverage of training configurations. When all training runs lie on a single ray D=k​ND=kN in the (N,D)(N,D) plane, the predictor variables become collinear, and combined with the empirically common near-equality of the NN and DD exponents this renders the scaling-law parameters practically unidentifiable. We prove this for four scaling-law formalisms - Chinchilla, repeated-data (muennighoff2023scaling), Kaplan (kaplan2020scaling), and Droppo-Elibol (droppo2021scaling) - via Gauss-Newton analysis. Because the degeneracy is in the Jacobian geometry rather than in the loss, any smooth estimation objective inherits the same ill-conditioning (Section 3). The law becomes a “sloppy” model (Section 2): a near-continuum of parameters fits training data indistinguishably yet diverges off the training ray. This directly corrupts isoFLOP prediction: isoFLOP curves cut across the training ray and thereby probe the sloppy direction that collinear fitting leaves unconstrained. Constructively, we give an identified reduced model recovering the combined effect along a single ray (Definition 2), and show empirically that non-collinear designs beat collinear ones when evaluated on the same held-out models (Section 4).

Key contributions. (i) A Gauss-Newton analysis proving that collinear designs are inherently ill-conditioned when the exponents governing model size and data size are close, with the condition number growing as the inverse square of the exponent gap - established for four scaling-law formalisms, with a corresponding confidence-interval inflation result (Proposition 1, Corollary 1); (ii) a closed-form TPP-diversity threshold that is necessary and sufficient for well-conditioned estimation (Proposition 2); (iii) a holdout-prediction ordering separating collinear from non-collinear designs (Theorem 1), validated at a 97.3%97.3\% win rate; (iv) an identified reduced parametrisation that recovers what a single-ray design can constrain (Definition 2); and (v) a fully reproducible experimental suite - ∼1,900{\sim}1{,}900 trained LLMs, all checkpoints, training metrics, accompanied by training and analysis code - provided via an anonymized live online repository link; supplementary material includes a ZIP file with a screenshot of that repository.11 1 Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Tokens-per-Parameter_Coverage_Is_Critical_for_Robust_LLM_Scaling_Law_Extrapolation-CC76. Checkpoints and metrics: https://huggingface.co/datasets/TPPIsCriticalFor/colinear_scaling_models.

Paper road-map. The rest of this paper is as follows. Section 3 develops the Gauss-Newton framework, proves condition-number bounds for the four formalisms under collinear designs, derives confidence-interval inflation for individual scale coefficients, and establishes the isoFLOP prediction-error amplification that separates collinear from non-collinear training; proofs are in Appendix B. Section 4 validates the analysis with controlled experiments across five corpora, four laws, and multiple precision regimes. Section 5 synthesises the empirical patterns and cautions against interpreting separate data versus model contributions from single-ray fits.

2 Related work

Predictable power-law scaling of generalization error was first reported by hestness2017deep and formalized for autoregressive language models by kaplan2020scaling using bivariate fits whose grids were often close to fixed-TPP for large subsets. bahri2024explaining linked the observed exponents to data-manifold structure via variance - and resolution-limited regimes. Follow-ups to Chinchilla examined data availability (villalobos2022will), overtraining (touvron2023llama), and unbounded compute with fixed data (kim2025pretraining); we extend our analysis to repeated-data regimes (muennighoff2023scaling) in Appendix B.7. sardana2024beyond sweep ratios up to 10,00010{,}000 TPP, producing inherently non-collinear designs that our diagnosis predicts should be well-identified (Section 3) - yet the most widely cited scaling-law parameters were estimated under the collinearity conditions we formalize. besiroglu2024chinchilla could not reconcile Chinchilla’s reported estimates with two of three replication methods, and porian2024resolving attribute the Kaplan-Chinchilla discrepancy to minor recipe differences (last-layer cost, warm-up, scale-dependent tuning); our ill-conditioning result explains why such small perturbations shift coefficients by orders of magnitude. Reinforcing this, bergsma2025powerlines show even optimizer hyperparameters (weight decay, batch size) obey power laws in the TPP ratio D/ND/N, so fixing a single ray couples recipe with scale. Concurrently, volkova2026robust report that fitting separate Chinchilla-style laws across optimizers yields ill-conditioned, highly correlated parameters - the same pathology we formalize from Jacobian geometry, observed along the optimizer axis. schaeffer2025pretraining propose sidestepping multicollinearity via compute-envelope or gold-reference parameterizations - both abandon the (N,D)(N,D) decomposition. zhang2026prescriptive pursue a related goal at the downstream-evaluation level, estimating compute-to-capability boundaries via quantile regression on post-trained models. Our work is complementary: we prove the condition number grows as Θ⁡(ε−2)\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}) in the exponent gap from Jacobian geometry alone (Proposition 1, Lemma 2), and give designs that restore identifiability within the multivariate framework (Proposition 4). yue2025relative’s Relative-Based Scaling Law is largely a single-axis sweep in model size, which our analysis flags as insufficient for multivariate identifiability. Farseer (li2025farseer) adds an NN-DD coupling term and trains ∼1,000\sim\!1{,}000 models on a diverse (N,D)(N,D) grid - the two-dimensional coverage our analysis requires - reporting a 433%433\% reduction in extrapolation error over Chinchilla; even such interaction terms remain unidentifiable under D=k​ND=kN (Section 3; Appendix B.16). shukor2025datamixtures similarly extend scaling laws to data-mixture weights, enlarging the multivariate design space where collinearity matters. hu2026neuneu sidestep parametric fitting altogether by training a neural extrapolator over checkpoint trajectories - orthogonal to our diagnosis of why the parametric fit is fragile. Statistically, the pathology we analyze is the nonlinear-regression analog of multicollinearity (kim2019multicollinearity; vatcheva2016multicollinearity; dormann2013collinearity; montgomery2012introduction; obrien2007caution) and of the “sloppy” model phenomenon (transtrum2010nonlinear; transtrum2015perspective), in which narrow model-manifold cross-sections yield fragile estimates - here induced by fixed-TPP sampling.

3 Formal analysis

The standard Chinchilla scaling law (hoffmann2022training, Eq. 2) approximates the loss as a sum of two power-law terms - capturing limited model capacity and data size - plus an irreducible loss EE, a form observed across deep learning domains (hestness2017deep; kaplan2020scaling, Sec. 3):

L⁡(N,D)=A​N−α+B​D−β+E,L(N,D)=AN^{-\alpha}+BD^{-\beta}+E, (1)

where A,B,α,β,E∈ℝ>0A,B,\alpha,\beta,E\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} and N,D∈ℝ>0N,D\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}.

Definition 1 (Scaling-law experimental dataset).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a training scheme (architecture, optimizer, algorithm, etc.). Each experiment records loss LiL_{i} for a model of size NiN_{i} on DiD_{i} tokens, yielding 𝒟={(Ni,Di,Li)}i=1m\mathcal{D}=\{(N_{i},D_{i},L_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m}. Let N1<⋯<Nn∈ℕ>0N_{1}<\cdots<N_{n}\in\mathbb{N}_{>0} be the model sizes and k1<⋯<kK∈ℝ>0k_{1}<\cdots<k_{K}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} the TPP ratios. A collinear design pairs each (Ni,kℓ)(N_{i},k_{\ell}) as (Ni,kℓ​Ni,Li​ℓ)(N_{i},\,k_{\ell}N_{i},\,L_{i\ell}), so m=n​Km=nK; the special case K=1K=1 is fully collinear. A parametric law L^​(N,D,𝜽)\hat{L}(N,D;\boldsymbol{\theta}) with 𝜽∈ℝp\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is fit to 𝒟\mathcal{D} by minimizing the discrepancy between predicted and observed losses; observations are split into a training set 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} and a holdout ℋ\mathcal{H} of nℋn_{\mathcal{H}} points (possibly at TPP ratios off the training manifold).

On a single ray (K=1K=1) - the dominant practical case (k≈20k\approx 20 for Chinchilla (hoffmann2022training; villalobos2022will)) - substituting D=k​ND=kN into (1) gives L⁡(N,k​N)=A​N−α+B​k−β​N−β+EL(N,kN)=AN^{-\alpha}+Bk^{-\beta}N^{-\beta}+E. Setting β=α\beta=\alpha collapses the two power-law terms, yielding a reduced model:

Definition 2 (Reduced Chinchilla model under fixed TPP).
L⁡(N,ψ,α,E)=(A+B​k−α)​N−α+E=ψ​N−α+E,L(N;\,\psi,\alpha,E)\;=\;\left(A+Bk^{-\alpha}\right)N^{-\alpha}+E\;=\;\psi N^{-\alpha}+E, (2)

where ψ≔A+B​k−α\psi\coloneqq A+B\,k^{-\alpha} combines the Chinchilla-scale coefficients from (1) and k∈ℝ>0k\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} is the fixed TPP ratio on that ray.

Definition 3 (Exponent gap by scaling law).

Define ε\varepsilon as a law-specific exponent gap in each law’s native notation (see Table 1): Chinchilla (and repeated-data on effective (N′,D′)(N^{\prime},D^{\prime})): ε≔|α−β|\varepsilon\coloneqq|\alpha-\beta|; Kaplan (exponents αN,αD\alpha_{N},\alpha_{D}): ε≔|αD−αN|\varepsilon\coloneqq|\alpha_{D}-\alpha_{N}|; Droppo-Elibol (exponents αN,αD,α\alpha_{N},\alpha_{D},\alpha with γN≔αN/α,γD≔αD/α\gamma_{N}\coloneqq\alpha_{N}/\alpha,\;\gamma_{D}\coloneqq\alpha_{D}/\alpha, α>0\alpha>0): ε≔|γN−γD|\varepsilon\coloneqq|\gamma_{N}-\gamma_{D}|. For example, Chinchilla reports α≈0.34\alpha\approx 0.34 and β≈0.28\beta\approx 0.28; Kaplan-scale fits use αN≈0.076\alpha_{N}\approx 0.076 and αD≈0.095\alpha_{D}\approx 0.095.

3.1 Gauss-Newton (GN) framework on a single ray

We fit by nonlinear least squares: minimize S⁡(𝜽)≔12​‖𝐫⁡(𝜽)‖2S(\boldsymbol{\theta})\coloneqq\tfrac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{r}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\|^{2} over 𝜽∈ℝp\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, where the residuals ri≔Li−L^​(Ni,Di,𝜽)r_{i}\coloneqq L_{i}-\hat{L}(N_{i},D_{i};\boldsymbol{\theta}) stack into 𝐫⁡(𝜽)\mathbf{r}(\boldsymbol{\theta}), with Jacobian J∈ℝm×pJ\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p} given by Ji​j=∂ri/∂θjJ_{ij}=\partial r_{i}/\partial\theta_{j}. We write κ⁡(M)≔λmax​(M)/λmin​(M)\kappa(M)\coloneqq\lambda_{\max}(M)/\lambda_{\min}(M) for the condition number of a symmetric positive-definite matrix MM. GN linearizes 𝐫\mathbf{r}, giving the normal equations (JT​J)​Δ​𝜽=−JT​𝐫(J^{T}J)\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}=-J^{T}\mathbf{r} (Appendix B.1). For each law’s scale coefficients (A,B)(A,B), let κA,B≔κ⁡((JT​J)A,B)\kappa_{A,B}\coloneqq\kappa\!\bigl((J^{T}J)_{A,B}\bigr) on the (A,B)(A,B) principal submatrix of JT​JJ^{T}J. Throughout the paper, we assume the (A,B)(A,B) pair is the dominant source of ill-conditioning in JT​JJ^{T}J (verified case-by-case in Appendices B.5-B.9), so κ⁡(JT​J)≍κA,B\kappa(J^{T}J)\asymp\kappa_{A,B} and the two are used interchangeably in the formal statements that follow. This dominance turns the lower bounds of Propositions 1-2 and Corollary 1 into matching two-sided (Θ\Theta) rates.

Proposition 1 (Full-matrix conditioning).

Let J∈ℝm×pJ\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p} have columns 𝐣1,…,𝐣p\mathbf{j}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{j}_{p}, and suppose two columns a≠ba\neq b satisfy 𝐣b=c​𝐣a+𝛅\mathbf{j}_{b}=c\,\mathbf{j}_{a}+\boldsymbol{\delta} with c≠0c\neq 0 and ‖𝛅‖=O⁡(ε)\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|=O(\varepsilon) for some scalar cc and 𝛅∈ℝm\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, where ε\varepsilon is the law-specific exponent gap (Definition 3). Let λmax​(JT​J)\lambda_{\max}(J^{T}J) and λmin​(JT​J)\lambda_{\min}(J^{T}J) denote the largest and smallest eigenvalues of JT​JJ^{T}J. Then as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, λmax​(JT​J)=Θ⁡(1)\lambda_{\max}(J^{T}J)=\Theta(1), λmin​(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε2)\lambda_{\min}(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{2}), and

κ⁡(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε−2).\kappa(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}). (3)

Proof. Appendix B.3. The bound applies to all four laws in Table 1: on a collinear ray D=k​ND=kN, every law’s Jacobian satisfies the near-proportionality assumption of Proposition 1 (Appendices B.5-B.9).

On a single ray, the reduced model (2) is identified (Proposition 4) while the full model is ill-conditioned (Proposition 1). The LS estimator’s uncertainty comes from inverting JT​JJ^{T}J (bjorck1996numerical, §2.8.3, eq. (2.8.7), p. 118): when the data cannot distinguish AA from BB, only their combination ψ\psi is pinned down, leaving each coefficient individually highly uncertain. The confidence interval on AA therefore widens by a factor Θ⁡(ε−1)\Theta(\varepsilon^{-1}) relative to the one on ψ\psi:

Corollary 1 (Confidence interval inflation).

Under i.i.d. Gaussian noise with variance σ2\sigma^{2}, on a single ray D=k​ND=kN, the least-squares confidence intervals for AA in the full Chinchilla model (1) and for the combined coefficient ψ\psi in the reduced model (2) satisfy, as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0,

CI0.95​(A)CI0.95​(ψ)=Θ⁡(ε−1).\frac{\mathrm{CI}_{0.95}(A)}{\mathrm{CI}_{0.95}(\psi)}\;=\;\Theta\!\left(\varepsilon^{-1}\right). (4)

Proof. Appendix B.11.

The approximated CI inflation for the four scaling laws is collected in Table 2.

3.2 Multi-ray designs and holdout prediction

We generalize to K≥1K\geq 1 collinear rays - the practically relevant setting of training at several TPP ratios - and ask how much TPP diversity suffices to restore well-conditioned estimation.

Proposition 2 (TPP diversity and full-matrix conditioning).

For any of the four scaling laws in Table 1, assume observed losses have i.i.d. Gaussian residuals with variance σ2\sigma^{2} (well-specified law). For any κtarget>0\kappa_{\mathrm{target}}>0 and ordered training ratios k1≤⋯≤kKk_{1}\leq\cdots\leq k_{K} (K≥1K\geq 1), to leading order as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, we have

κ⁡(JT​J)≤κtarget⇔1K​∑ℓ=1Kkℓ−2​βeff−(1K​∑ℓ=1Kkℓ−βeff)2⏟VK≥(K+∑ℓ=1Kkℓ−2​βeff)2K2​κtarget⏟τK,\kappa(J^{T}J)\leq\kappa_{\mathrm{target}}\iff\underbrace{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}k_{\ell}^{-2\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}}\;-\;\left(\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}k_{\ell}^{-\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}}\right)^{\!2}}_{V_{K}}\;\;\geq\;\;\underbrace{\frac{\displaystyle\Bigl(K+\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}k_{\ell}^{-2\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}}\Bigr)^{\!2}}{K^{2}\;\kappa_{\mathrm{target}}}}_{\tau_{K}}, (5)

where VKV_{K} is the second central moment (or variance) of {kℓ−βeff}ℓ=1K\{k_{\ell}^{-\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}}\}_{\ell=1}^{K}, and βeff\beta_{\mathrm{eff}} is the law-specific data-size exponent: β\beta for Chinchilla/repeated-data, αD\alpha_{D} for Kaplan, γD\gamma_{D} for Droppo-Elibol. For K=1K=1, V1=0<τ1V_{1}=0<\tau_{1}, so (5) never holds; for K=2K=2 with R≔k2/k1R\coloneqq k_{2}/k_{1} it reduces to R≥RminR\geq R_{\min} (Eq. (95), Table 9); for K>2K>2 interior rays reduce VKV_{K} at fixed endpoint spread, so K=2K=2 with mass at the endpoints is near-optimal at fixed RR and K≥3K\geq 3 does not relax the spread requirement (Appendix B.15).

Proof. Appendix B.12; explicit VK,τKV_{K},\tau_{K} algebra and the two-ray reduction are in Appendix B.15.

With K≥2K\geq 2 training rays, per-ray (A,B)(A,B) collinearity (Proposition 1) is cured at the full-matrix level iff VK≥τKV_{K}\geq\tau_{K} (Proposition 2). Since (5) can be evaluated before training using a literature estimate of βeff\beta_{\mathrm{eff}} (the data-side power-law exponent governing L∝D−βeffL\propto D^{-\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}} at leading order; e.g. β≈0.28\beta\approx 0.28 for Chinchilla), it is an a-priori design diagnostic. Theorem 1 translates the conditioning into a holdout-RMSE ordering.

Theorem 1 (Holdout prediction regimes).

Under Proposition 2, assume κtarget\kappa_{\mathrm{target}} is small enough that κ⁡(JT​J)≤κtarget\kappa(J^{T}J)\leq\kappa_{\mathrm{target}} ensures numerically well-conditioned NLS and faithful Gauss-Newton linearization (Appendix B.13). Let CO denote a collinear design (K≥1K\geq 1), NC a non-collinear design with at least two distinct training ratios and dense two-dimensional (N,D)(N,D) coverage, and let ℋ\mathcal{H} denote a holdout with a nonzero fraction of off-ratio points (k′=D′/N′k^{\prime}=D^{\prime}/N^{\prime} differs from every training ratio). For X∈{CO,NC}\mathrm{X}\in\{\mathrm{CO},\mathrm{NC}\}, RMSEℋX\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\mathrm{X}} is the root-mean-square prediction error of L^\hat{L} on ℋ\mathcal{H} under that training design, and Rℋ2​XR^{2\,\mathrm{X}}_{\mathcal{H}} the corresponding coefficient of determination on ℋ\mathcal{H}. The regimes below hold at leading order as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

Regime A (ill-conditioned, VK<τKV_{K}<\tau_{K}; for the CO ray design, includes all K=1K=1 and any K≥2K\geq 2 with insufficient diversity):

𝔼⁡[RMSEℋNC]<𝔼⁡[RMSEℋCO],\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\mathrm{NC}}]<\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\mathrm{CO}}], (6)

and thus 𝔼⁡[Rℋ2​NC]>𝔼⁡[Rℋ2​CO]\mathbb{E}[R^{2\,\mathrm{NC}}_{\mathcal{H}}]>\mathbb{E}[R^{2\,\mathrm{CO}}_{\mathcal{H}}] (misspecification extension: Appendix B.13).

Regime B (well-conditioned, VK≥τKV_{K}\geq\tau_{K}; requires K≥2K\geq 2):  𝔼⁡[RMSEℋCO]/𝔼⁡[RMSEℋNC]=Θ⁡(1)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\mathrm{CO}}]/\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\mathrm{NC}}]=\Theta(1), i.e., neither design has systematic asymptotic RMSE dominance.

Proof. Appendix B.13 (Gauss-Newton linearization, spectral decomposition, RMSE ordering).

3.3 Applying to respective scaling laws

Table 1 collects the collinear pair, Jacobian columns on a single ray D=kℓ​ND=k_{\ell}N, and exponent gap for each law. Proposition 1 then yields κ⁡(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε−2)\kappa(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}) in all four cases; per-law derivations are in Appendices B.5, B.7, B.8, and B.9. The resulting CI inflation is statistical (Corollary 1); per-law factors appear in Table 2. First, Kaplan is the most degenerate under single-TPP: its gap 0.0190.019 is ∼3×\sim 3\times smaller than Chinchilla’s 0.060.06, amplifying ε−2\varepsilon^{-2} by an order of magnitude (∼2.7×103\sim 2.7{\times}10^{3} vs. ∼278\sim 278) and CI inflation by ∼3×\sim 3\times (∼53×\sim 53\times vs. ∼17×\sim 17\times) - matching its strong empirical degeneracy. Second, Chinchilla and repeated-data are problematic: small, near-equal exponents (α,β<0.4\alpha,\beta<0.4) yield CI inflation ∼17×\sim 17\times, leaving individual A,BA,B estimates noise-dominated. Third, Droppo-Elibol is fit-dependent: for language data |γN−γD||\gamma_{N}-\gamma_{D}| is comparable to Chinchilla’s 0.060.06, and the well-identified outer envelope (α,L∞)(\alpha,L_{\infty}) does not relieve the (NC,DC)(N_{C},D_{C}) degeneracy. The reduced model (Definition 2) is therefore most critical for Kaplan- and Chinchilla-class fits, with Kaplan the most degenerate.

3.4 IsoFLOP prediction under collinearity

IsoFLOP curves are contours of constant training compute C=6​N​DC=6ND (hoffmann2022training). They cut across the training ray and probe the sloppy parameter direction that collinear training leaves unconstrained, making them an informative diagnostic.

Definition 4 (Induced isoFLOP curves plot).

Let L^​(N,D,𝜽)\hat{L}(N,D;\boldsymbol{\theta}) be a fitted scaling law and ℋ={(Ni,Di,Li)}i=1nℋ\mathcal{H}=\{(N_{i},D_{i},L_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n_{\mathcal{H}}} a holdout set of size nℋn_{\mathcal{H}} with induced compute budgets Ci≔6​Ni​DiC_{i}\coloneqq 6N_{i}D_{i}. The induced isoFLOP curves are the family

{N↦L^​(N,Ci/(6​N),𝜽):N∈[Nmin,Nmax]}i=1nℋ,\{N\mapsto\hat{L}(N,C_{i}/(6N);\boldsymbol{\theta})\,:\,N\in[N_{\min},N_{\max}]\}_{i=1}^{n_{\mathcal{H}}}, (7)

with Nmin≔minj⁡NjN_{\min}\coloneqq\min_{j}N_{j} and Nmax≔maxj⁡NjN_{\max}\coloneqq\max_{j}N_{j}. The induced isoFLOP curves plot draws this family on the (N,L)(N,L)-plane with each holdout point (Ni,Li)(N_{i},L_{i}) overlaid on its curve.

Proposition 3 (RMSE invariance under isoFLOP reparameterization).

With L^,ℋ,{Ci}\hat{L},\mathcal{H},\{C_{i}\} as in Definition 4, the RMSE of L^\hat{L} on ℋ\mathcal{H} is invariant under (N,D)↦(N,C)(N,D)\mapsto(N,C): evaluating the ii-th induced isoFLOP curve at N=NiN=N_{i} yields the same error as evaluating L^​(Ni,Di)\hat{L}(N_{i},D_{i}) directly (Appendix B.14).

4 Empirical evaluation

Empirically evaluating dense TPP coverage. To validate the formal statements of Section 3, we fit each scaling law under two training designs - collinear (CO) and non-collinear (NC) - and measure holdout error on a shared CO/NC split across five pre-training corpora: three common and two specialized (see Appendix C.5). All models are LLaMA-style transformers trained with AdamW on a cosine schedule; full hyperparameters are in Appendix C. Model sizes span 5.045.04-76.576.5M parameters across 14 log-spaced configurations (Nmax/Nmin≈15N_{\max}/N_{\min}\approx 15; see Table 10). Tokenization uses cl100k_base (V=100,277V{=}100{,}277), and NN counts all trainable parameters (embeddings included) per the Hoffmann-Chinchilla convention (hoffmann2022training); we apply this convention uniformly when fitting all four laws - including Kaplan (kaplan2020scaling), which originally defines NN on non-embedding parameters - and our analysis does not involve a FLOPs budget CC. We log cross-entropy loss per epoch. Experimental designs. Both designs share identical architectures, optimizers, and schedules; the only difference is how (N,D)(N,D) pairs are sampled, and total run counts are comparable. Collinear (CO): Every run sets D=k​ND=kN for k∈𝒦train≔{1, 1.5, 1.9, 2, 2.5, 2.7, 3, 3.3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5}k\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{train}}\coloneqq\{1,\;1.5,\;1.9,\;2,\;2.5,\;2.7,\;3,\;3.3,\;3.5,\;4,\;4.5,\;5\}. Although 12 ratios are used, each defines a ray through the origin; the configurations form a fan of rays rather than filling a two-dimensional region, producing the collinearity diagnosed in Section 3. Non-Collinear (NC): The same 14 model sizes are crossed with 12 dataset sizes (∼10\sim 10M-∼276\sim 276M tokens), yielding a 14×1214\times 12 grid spanning a two-dimensional region. The implied ratio k=D/Nk=D/N varies freely, decoupling the two axes and eliminating the rank deficiency. The grid is visualized in Appendix D.1. We fit the four mentioned scaling laws via nonlinear least squares with 100 random restarts and a differential-evolution polish, repeated across 30 independent optimizer seeds (see Appendix D.6). For Repeated-Data, each epoch’s checkpoint is a separate observation; for the remaining three we fit per-epoch losses independently (epochs 1, 2, 3). To verify robustness to numerical precision, we run a BF16 round (k∈𝒦traink\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{train}}, mixed precision). The NC advantage persists in this regime (Appendix D.4). Additionally, we provide a preliminary high-TPP experiment (small-scale, k∈𝒦big≔{10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15}k\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{big}}\coloneqq\{10,\,11,\,12,\,13,\,14,\,15\}, holdouts up to 2020) with Wikipedia and Chinchilla, achieving a 63.3%63.3\% NC win rate (CI [45.5%,78.1%][45.5\%,78.1\%]; see Appendices D.7 and C.8).

Evaluation splits. The collinear design reserves five TPP ratios k∈𝒦test≔{6, 6.2, 6.5, 6.7, 7}k\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{test}}\coloneqq\{6,\,6.2,\,6.5,\,6.7,\,7\}, forming a collinear holdout ℋcol\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{col}} on rays just beyond the training fan. The non-collinear design reserves dataset sizes D∈[300,401]D\in[300,401]\,M tokens, forming a non-collinear holdout ℋnc\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{nc}} that requires extrapolation into the (N,D)(N,D) plane beyond the training fan. We evaluate both designs on a single unified holdout ℋ=ℋcol∪ℋnc\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{col}}\cup\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{nc}}, so that every comparison is head-to-head, with test points from both geometries. All paper metrics and tables use this ℋ\mathcal{H} when reporting holdout performance; per-split breakdowns appear in Appendix D.

TPP coverage tracking. To quantify how design coverage affects fit quality, we incrementally widen each design’s data axis - progressively including additional TPP ratios (CO) or dataset sizes (NC) - and refit each scaling law at each step, recording holdout R2R^{2}. The coverage fraction reports the fraction of levels included: 1.01.0 means all of 𝒦train\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{train}} (CO) or all 1212 DD sizes (NC). Because the two designs draw from distinct value sets, CO and NC curves trace independent trajectories through the (N,D)(N,D) plane. Setup details and paired convergence plots appear in Appendices D.5 and D.8, respectively.

Aggregate metrics. Table 3 reports mean, median, and standard deviation of R2R^{2} and RMSE across all law-dataset combinations for each design-split pair. Table 4 tallies pairwise wins (higher R2R^{2} or lower RMSE) for NC vs. CO, broken down by dataset, law, and epoch mode. Table 5 confirms the effect is precision-invariant: under BF16 mixed-precision training on Wikipedia, NC achieves a unified holdout R2R^{2} of 0.9660.966 vs. CO’s 0.9410.941. The BF16 winrate (98.7%98.7\%, CI: [96.6%,99.5%][96.6\%,99.5\%]) is comparable to the full-precision results, presented in Appendix D.4 (Table 16). Full per-dataset breakdowns for FP and BF16 runs are in Appendices D and E.

Representative plots. Figure 1 complements the aggregate statistics with a representative three-panel view: fitted loss surface, holdout R2R^{2} vs. TPP coverage, and induced isoFLOP curves (more three-panel views in Appendix D.8). TPP coverage is the fraction of 𝒦train\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{train}} for CO (or available DD sizes for NC) included in the fit; see Section 4. The contrast is stark: the Kaplan CO fit on RedPajama (first-epoch loss) achieves a holdout R2R^{2} of only 0.510.51, while NC reaches 0.910.91. The surface panel (Figure 1(a)) shows CO residuals growing toward the small-NN region, where Proposition 1’s sloppy direction dominates predicted loss. The convergence panel (Figure 1(b)) aligns with the predictions of Theorem 1 and Corollary 1: (i) CO sits strictly below NC at every TPP coverage level because, at κtarget=100\kappa_{\mathrm{target}}=100, Kaplan’s full CO satisfies VK≈1.6×10−3≪τK≈3.4×10−2V_{K}\approx 1.6\times 10^{-3}\ll\tau_{K}\approx 3.4\times 10^{-2}, while NC yields VK≈9.3×10−3,τK≈3.1×10−2V_{K}\approx 9.3\times 10^{-3},\;\tau_{K}\approx 3.1\times 10^{-2} (Proposition 2); both sit in Regime A of Theorem 1, which predicts NC > CO (6); (ii) CO’s CI bars are ∼53×\sim 53\times wider than NC’s - matching the Θ⁡(ε−1)\Theta(\varepsilon^{-1}) inflation predicted by Corollary 1 (numerically ε−1≈53\varepsilon^{-1}\approx 53 at Kaplan’s ε≈0.019\varepsilon\approx 0.019; Table 2); (iii) CO’s bars shrink monotonically with coverage but never close the gap, because κ⁡(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε−2)\kappa(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}) (numerically ∼2.8×103\sim 2.8\times 10^{3}) is design-level, independent of nn (Proposition 1); (iv) CO’s central R2R^{2} oscillates while NC’s rises smoothly because Kaplan’s scale-coefficient estimates (N^c,D^c)(\hat{N}_{c},\hat{D}_{c}) wander along the sloppy direction of Proposition 1, whereas NC’s 2D coverage keeps κ⁡(JT​J)≤κtarget\kappa(J^{T}J)\leq\kappa_{\mathrm{target}} (Theorem 1), bounding the sloppy direction; (v) the isoFLOP panel (Figure 1(c)) makes the same separation visible at the budget level: CO’s dashed curves splay apart at high NN along the sloppy direction of Proposition 1, while NC’s solid curves stay tight.

Empirical evaluation of Theorem 1 through budget-matched subset enumeration. Table 6 supports Theorem 1, which predicts that within Regime A (VK<τKV_{K}<\tau_{K}; (6)) an NC design achieves smaller expected holdout RMSE than a budget-matched CO design. We enumerate all 212−1=4,0952^{12}-1=4{,}095 non-empty subsets S⊆{1,…,12}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,12\} of available TPP ratios. Each CO⁡(S)\mathrm{CO}(S) (Definition 10) is paired with a bounding-box NC design of identical cardinality (Appendix D.3) and classified a priori via VK<τK​(κtarget)V_{K}<\tau_{K}(\kappa_{\mathrm{target}}) using literature βeff\beta_{\mathrm{eff}} (Definition 3). Because the theorem doesn’t fix a single κtarget\kappa_{\mathrm{target}}, we average the NC-win rate over 2,0002{,}000 values drawn log-uniformly from [1,109][1,10^{9}]. Each κtarget\kappa_{\mathrm{target}} is repeated under 2222 seeds that vary the bounding-box construction and the random restarts of the fit optimizer (300300 restarts per fit; random 70%70\% subsample of ℋ\mathcal{H}). When Regime A is empty for a given κtarget\kappa_{\mathrm{target}}, that seed is skipped. NC beats CO consistently within Regime A for all three laws: 68.5%68.5\% (Chinchilla), 57.4%57.4\% (Droppo-Elibol), and 66.0%66.0\% (Kaplan) averaged across corpora, all with CIs excluding 50%50\%. The effect is strongest on the web-crawled corpora C4, RedPajama, and Wikipedia (NC wins 7777-88%88\% for Chinchilla); the two specialized corpora (Cosmopedia and peS2o) show systematically smaller margins, which we interpret as a scope limitation in Section 5.

5 Discussion and conclusions

The formal statements of Section 3 establish that collinear designs will produce deceptively confident fits that fail to generalize. The experiments of Section 4 confirm this statement quantitatively and reveal how severe the failure is in practice.

Collinear designs overfit, non-collinear designs generalize: on training data CO achieves higher R2R^{2} than NC in nearly every experiment (Table 3: aggregate 0.9850.985 vs. 0.9530.953), as a five-parameter fit along a 1D manifold near-interpolates, but on held-out data the ranking reverses - NC raises unified-holdout R2R^{2} from 0.8370.837 to 0.9320.932 and cuts RMSE from 0.2370.237 to 0.1560.156, with seed-paired per-trial RMSE gaps of 33-8×8\times that rule out an averaging artifact, sitting below Theorem 1’s Θ(ε−1)≈16.7×\Theta(\varepsilon^{-1})\approx 16.7\times ceiling at Chinchilla exponents (Eqs. (81)-(84)) with the slack absorbed by the design-independent misspecification floor (87). Scaling 12 TPP ratios does not rescue collinearity: our CO design spans 𝒦train\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{train}} (1212 ratios) yet NC still wins 97.3%97.3\% of 1,5001{,}500 seed-paired comparisons (Table 4) because κ∝ε−2\kappa\propto\varepsilon^{-2} depends on the exponent gap, not the number of rays (Proposition 1). The effect is precision-invariant: a BF16 mixed-precision replication on Wikipedia gives unified-holdout R2=0.966R^{2}=0.966 vs. CO’s 0.9410.941 (Table 5) and a seed-paired NC win rate of 98.7%98.7\% (296296/300300, 95%95\% CI [96.6%,99.5%][96.6\%,99.5\%]; Table 16), consistent with the FP32 Wikipedia win rate of 99.7%99.7\% (Table 4). The pattern is consistent across corpora, laws, and epochs: Table 4 reports NC win rates above 93%93\% on every corpus (min 93.0%93.0\% C4, max 100%100\% RedPajama), above 95%95\% for every scaling law, and above 93%93\% for every evaluation epoch. The combined takeaway is that single-TPP fits do not support coefficient-level interpretation - along D=k​ND=kN rays only the combined effect of NN and DD is well constrained, so claims such as “model size contributes XX% and data YY% of the reducible loss” require training to span a two-dimensional region of (N,D)(N,D), and even 12 collinear rays are insufficient (Table 3: CO’s training-R2R^{2} advantage flips to a 0.030.03-0.100.10 holdout deficit); when the design is collinear, the reduced parameterization (Definition 2) is the appropriate reporting target.

Limitations. Theorem 1 gives an ordering, not a quantitative gap, so the observed seed-paired RMSE spread is consistent with but not predicted by the theorem; under misspecification, a design-independent approximation-bias floor bounds the ratio (87). Corollary 1’s closed-form CI inflation assumes i.i.d. Gaussian residuals; checkpoint-level temporal correlation and shared-corpus noise would under-state, not invert, the pathology. Empirically, we use small-scale models (5.045.04-76.576.5M parameters), a single LLaMA-style architecture, English-only text, one run per (N,D)(N,D), and a single fitter (multi-start L-BFGS-B with DE polish; Appendices C, D.6). Training hyperparameters were not swept per-(N,D)(N,D); following gadre2024language we adopt a fixed recipe applied identically to CO and NC, so the head-to-head comparison is controlled even if absolute losses are not optimal. The budget-matched validation (Section 4, Table 6) softens to near-50%50\% on Cosmopedia and peS2o, plausibly due to non-power-law loss surfaces attenuating variance inflation (untested); Regime A transfers most cleanly to web-crawled and reference text. Finally, the analysis targets pre-training loss; downstream-task and cross-domain extensions (bhagia2025establishingtaskscalinglaws) inherit the Jacobian argument but are not validated here.

Safeguards. All corpora (C4, RedPajama, Wikipedia, Cosmopedia, peS2o) are public and pre-filtered; no new data collection. Released checkpoints (5.045.04-76.576.5M; Appendix C) are diagnostic data points, not deployable models, and the code targets scaling-law fitting and small-scale training runs, not serving production models. The paper’s deflationary posture against single-TPP coefficient claims offsets any marginal acceleration from better-identified scaling laws.

Broader impact. Scaling laws guide multi-billion-dollar pre-training decisions and inform claims about the relative importance of capacity vs. data volume; under single-TPP designs those claims are unidentifiable (Section 3, Corollary 1). Our diagnostics (Proposition 2, (5)) flag such fits, and the framework reframes the Kaplan-Chinchilla replication gap (besiroglu2024chinchilla; porian2024resolving) as a predictable consequence of Θ⁡(ε−2)\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}) ill-conditioning - AA’s CIs inflate ≥17×\geq\!17\times at Chinchilla exponents and ≥53×\geq\!53\times at Kaplan exponents (Table 2). Because the degeneracy is purely Jacobian-geometric, the analysis transfers to generative vision (henighan2020scaling; alabdulmohsin2022revisiting), time-series (edwards2024scaling; yao2024scaling), and scientific ML; IsoFLOP-grid designs (Section 3.4) naturally avoid the pitfall.

LLM usage. All research questions, results, design, and analyses originated with the authors. The primary non-trivial use of LLMs was as a sounding board for candidate proof steps: the authors drafted the structure of each derivation, asked an LLM to propose intermediate algebraic manipulations or identities, and then independently verified, rewrote, or discarded each suggestion before incorporation. Auxiliary uses included exposition, LaTeX typesetting, boilerplate code, and prose editing, all reviewed by the authors. LLMs did not generate any claims, theorems, or experimental conclusions. We acknowledge Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7 for its assistance in this capacity.

B.1 Appendix - Derivation of the Gauss-Newton normal equations

This subsection provides a self-contained derivation of the Gauss-Newton normal equations from the nonlinear least-squares objective (Section 3.1), following the treatment in (nocedal2006numerical, Chap. 10).

Step 1: Objective and gradient. Recall the objective:

S⁡(𝜽)=12​‖𝐫⁡(𝜽)‖2=12​∑i=1mri​(𝜽)2,S(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\|\mathbf{r}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\|^{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\sum_{i=1}^{m}r_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{2}, (8)

where ri​(𝜽)=Li−L^​(Ni,Di,𝜽)r_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=L_{i}-\hat{L}(N_{i},D_{i};\boldsymbol{\theta}). The gradient with respect to 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} is obtained by the chain rule:

∂S∂θj=∑i=1mri(𝜽)∂ri∂θj=−∑i=1mri(𝜽)∂L^i∂θj,\frac{\partial S}{\partial\theta_{j}}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}r_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\;\frac{\partial r_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}}=-\sum_{i=1}^{m}r_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\;\frac{\partial\hat{L}_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}}, (9)

since ∂ri/∂θj=−∂L^i/∂θj\partial r_{i}/\partial\theta_{j}=-\partial\hat{L}_{i}/\partial\theta_{j}. Define the residual Jacobian (equivalently, predictions satisfy ∂ri/∂θj=−∂L^i/∂θj\partial r_{i}/\partial\theta_{j}=-\partial\hat{L}_{i}/\partial\theta_{j}):

J∈ℝm×p,Ji​j≔−∂L^​(Ni,Di,𝜽)∂θj=∂ri∂θj.J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p},\hskip 18.49988ptJ_{ij}\coloneqq-\frac{\partial\hat{L}(N_{i},D_{i};\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\theta_{j}}=\frac{\partial r_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}}. (10)

Thus Ji​j=∂ri/∂θjJ_{ij}=\partial r_{i}/\partial\theta_{j}, matching Section 3.1. With this convention, the gradient (9) can be written in matrix form as:

∇𝜽S=JT​𝐫​(𝜽).\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}S=J^{T}\mathbf{r}(\boldsymbol{\theta}). (11)

Step 2: Linearisation of the residuals. At a current iterate 𝜽k\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k}, expand each residual to first order in the step Δ​𝜽=𝜽−𝜽k\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}=\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k}:

ri​(𝜽k+Δ​𝜽)≈ri​(𝜽k)+∑j=1p∂ri∂θj|𝜽k​Δ​θj=ri,k+(Jk​Δ​𝜽)i,r_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k}+\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta})\approx r_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k})+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{\partial r_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}}\bigg|_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k}}\!\!\Delta\theta_{j}=r_{i,k}+(J_{k}\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta})_{i}, (12)

where ri,k≔ri​(𝜽k)r_{i,k}\coloneqq r_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k}) and Jk≔J⁡(𝜽k)J_{k}\coloneqq J(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k}) is the Jacobian evaluated at 𝜽k\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k}. In vector notation:

𝐫⁡(𝜽k+Δ​𝜽)≈𝐫k+Jk​Δ​𝜽.\mathbf{r}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k}+\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta})\approx\mathbf{r}_{k}+J_{k}\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}. (13)

Step 3: Substitute into the objective. Substituting (13) into (8):

S⁡(𝜽k+Δ​𝜽)\displaystyle S(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k}+\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}) ≈12​‖𝐫k+Jk​Δ​𝜽‖2\displaystyle\approx\tfrac{1}{2}\,\|\mathbf{r}_{k}+J_{k}\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^{2}
=12​(𝐫k+Jk​Δ​𝜽)T​(𝐫k+Jk​Δ​𝜽)\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\bigl(\mathbf{r}_{k}+J_{k}\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}\bigr)^{T}\bigl(\mathbf{r}_{k}+J_{k}\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}\bigr)
=12​𝐫kT​𝐫k+𝐫kT​Jk​Δ​𝜽+12​Δ​𝜽T​JkT​Jk​Δ​𝜽.\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{r}_{k}^{T}\mathbf{r}_{k}+\mathbf{r}_{k}^{T}J_{k}\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}^{T}J_{k}^{T}J_{k}\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}.

This is an exact quadratic in Δ​𝜽\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta} (no higher-order terms remain because the linearization has already been applied). Denote this quadratic model as mk​(Δ​𝜽)m_{k}(\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}).

Step 4: Stationarity condition. At the minimizer of mkm_{k}, the gradient with respect to Δ​𝜽\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta} vanishes:

∇Δ​𝜽mk\displaystyle\nabla_{\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}}\,m_{k} =JkT​𝐫k+JkT​Jk​Δ​𝜽=𝟎,\displaystyle=J_{k}^{T}\mathbf{r}_{k}+J_{k}^{T}J_{k}\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}=\mathbf{0}, (14)
(JkT​Jk)​Δ​𝜽\displaystyle(J_{k}^{T}J_{k})\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta} =−JkT​𝐫k.\displaystyle=-J_{k}^{T}\mathbf{r}_{k}. (15)

This is the Gauss-Newton normal equation. When JkT​JkJ_{k}^{T}J_{k} is non-singular, the unique solution is Δ​𝜽=−(JkT​Jk)−1​JkT​𝐫k\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}=-(J_{k}^{T}J_{k})^{-1}J_{k}^{T}\mathbf{r}_{k}, and the parameter update is 𝜽k+1=𝜽k+Δ​𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k+1}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k}+\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}.

Remark 1 (Relationship to the full Hessian.).

The exact Hessian of SS is:

H⁡(𝜽)=∇2S=JT​J+Q,Q≔∑i=1mri​∇2ri.H(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\nabla^{2}S=J^{T}J+Q,\hskip 18.49988ptQ\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{m}r_{i}\,\nabla^{2}r_{i}. (16)

The Gauss-Newton method drops the second-order correction QQ, replacing HH with the Gauss-Newton approximation JT​JJ^{T}J. This is justified when ‖𝐫‖\|\mathbf{r}\| is small (so Q≈0Q\approx 0) or when the model is approximately linear in 𝛉\boldsymbol{\theta} (so ∇2ri≈0\nabla^{2}r_{i}\approx 0). For the Chinchilla and repeated-data scaling laws, L^\hat{L} is linear in the scale coefficients AA and BB, so ∇A,B2ri=0\nabla^{2}_{A,B}r_{i}=0 exactly and QA,B=0Q_{A,B}=0: the Gauss-Newton and full Newton curvatures coincide in the (A,B)(A,B) sub-block regardless of residual magnitudes.

Remark 2 (Why JT​JJ^{T}J controls identifiability.).

When JT​JJ^{T}J is well conditioned, the normal equations (15) have a unique, numerically stable solution. When two columns of JJ are nearly proportional, JT​JJ^{T}J becomes nearly singular:

λmin​(JT​J)→0⟹‖(JT​J)−1‖→∞,\lambda_{\min}(J^{T}J)\to 0\hskip 9.24994pt\Longrightarrow\hskip 9.24994pt\|(J^{T}J)^{-1}\|\to\infty, (17)

and the step Δ​𝛉\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta} becomes unbounded in the direction of the near-null eigenvector. Under i.i.d. noise with variance σ2\sigma^{2}, one has

Cov⁡(𝜽^)=σ2​(JT​J)−1\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\sigma^{2}\,(J^{T}J)^{-1} (18)

in the linear least-squares case (Lemma 1), and the same expression approximates the large-sample covariance for nonlinear least squares (Remark 3); thus the parameter variances along the near-null direction scale as σ2/λmin​(JT​J)\sigma^{2}/\lambda_{\min}(J^{T}J). This is the statistical manifestation of the ill-conditioning: any parameter combination aligned with the sloppy direction of JT​JJ^{T}J is effectively unconstrained by the data. The remainder of Section 3 shows that, on each single collinear ray D=kℓ​ND=k_{\ell}N, the scale-coefficient columns of JJ are nearly proportional whenever ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1 (the law-specific exponent gap of Definition 3; e.g., |α−β||\alpha-\beta| for Chinchilla), driving λmin​(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε2)\lambda_{\min}(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{2}) and hence κ⁡(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε−2)\kappa(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}). With K>1K>1 rays, the bound applies ray-by-ray; the design escapes ill-conditioning only when the TPP diversity VK≥τKV_{K}\geq\tau_{K} in (5) (Proposition 2). For K=2K=2, this requires a sufficient endpoint spread R=kK/k1R=k_{K}/k_{1} (Eq. (95) and Table 9).

B.2 Appendix - Covariance under homoscedastic i.i.d. noise

Lemma 1 (Parameter covariance in linear least squares).

For any 𝐌∈ℝm×p\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p} of full column rank and 𝛉⋆∈ℝp\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, suppose

Li=(𝐌𝜽⋆)i+ϵi,i=1,…,m,L_{i}=(\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\star})_{i}+\epsilon_{i},\hskip 18.49988pti=1,\dots,m,

where {ϵi}i=1m\{\epsilon_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} are i.i.d. with mean zero and variance σ2\sigma^{2}. Let 𝛉^\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} minimize ∑i=1m(Li−(𝐌​𝛉)i)2\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigl(L_{i}-(\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\theta})_{i}\bigr)^{2}, and let J∈ℝm×pJ\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p} be the Jacobian of the residuals ri​(𝛉)≔Li−(𝐌​𝛉)ir_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\coloneqq L_{i}-(\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\theta})_{i} with respect to 𝛉\boldsymbol{\theta} (holding 𝐌\mathbf{M} fixed). Then J=−𝐌J=-\mathbf{M} and

Cov⁡(𝜽^)=σ2​(JT​J)−1.\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\sigma^{2}\,(J^{T}J)^{-1}. (19)
Proof.

Differentiating ri​(𝜽)=Li−∑j=1pMi​j​θjr_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=L_{i}-\sum_{j=1}^{p}M_{ij}\,\theta_{j} gives ∂ri/∂θj=−Mi​j\partial r_{i}/\partial\theta_{j}=-M_{ij}, hence J=−𝐌J=-\mathbf{M} and JT​J=𝐌T​𝐌J^{T}J=\mathbf{M}^{T}\mathbf{M}. The normal equations yield 𝐌T​𝐌​𝜽^=𝐌T​𝐋\mathbf{M}^{T}\mathbf{M}\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\mathbf{M}^{T}\mathbf{L} with 𝐋≔(L1,…,Lm)T\mathbf{L}\coloneqq(L_{1},\dots,L_{m})^{T}, so

𝜽^=(𝐌T​𝐌)−1​𝐌T​𝐋.\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=(\mathbf{M}^{T}\mathbf{M})^{-1}\mathbf{M}^{T}\mathbf{L}.

Substituting 𝐋=𝐌​𝜽⋆+ϵ\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\star}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon} with ϵ≔(ϵ1,…,ϵm)T\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\coloneqq(\epsilon_{1},\dots,\epsilon_{m})^{T}:

𝜽^−𝜽⋆=(𝐌T​𝐌)−1​𝐌T​ϵ.\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\star}=(\mathbf{M}^{T}\mathbf{M})^{-1}\mathbf{M}^{T}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}.

Because 𝔼⁡[ϵ]=𝟎\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]=\mathbf{0}, also 𝔼⁡[𝜽^]=𝜽⋆\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}]=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\star}. Because Cov⁡(ϵ)=σ2​Im\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\sigma^{2}I_{m},

Cov⁡(𝜽^)\displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) =(𝐌T​𝐌)−1​𝐌T​(σ2​Im)​𝐌​(𝐌T​𝐌)−1\displaystyle=(\mathbf{M}^{T}\mathbf{M})^{-1}\mathbf{M}^{T}(\sigma^{2}I_{m})\,\mathbf{M}\,(\mathbf{M}^{T}\mathbf{M})^{-1}
=σ2​(𝐌T​𝐌)−1=σ2​(JT​J)−1.∎\displaystyle=\sigma^{2}\,(\mathbf{M}^{T}\mathbf{M})^{-1}=\sigma^{2}\,(J^{T}J)^{-1}.\qed
Remark 3 (Nonlinear least squares).

Lemma 1 applies directly when the predictor L^​(Ni,Di,𝛉)\hat{L}(N_{i},D_{i};\boldsymbol{\theta}) is affine in 𝛉\boldsymbol{\theta} on the design (e.g., fitting (A,B,E)(A,B,E) in (1) with (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) held fixed). For general nonlinear L^\hat{L}, the same matrix σ2​(JT​J)−1\sigma^{2}(J^{T}J)^{-1} with Ji​j=∂ri/∂θjJ_{ij}=\partial r_{i}/\partial\theta_{j} evaluated at the true parameter is the standard large-sample approximation to Cov⁡(𝛉^)\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) under regularity conditions for nonlinear least squares (bates1988nonlinear).

B.3 Appendix - Proof of Proposition 1 (Full-Matrix Conditioning)

Proposition (Full-matrix conditioning - full statement; restated from Proposition 1).

Let J∈ℝm×pJ\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p} be the Jacobian of the residuals with columns 𝐣1,…,𝐣p∈ℝm\mathbf{j}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{j}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} (i.e., J=[𝐣1​∣⋯∣​𝐣p]J=[\,\mathbf{j}_{1}\mid\cdots\mid\mathbf{j}_{p}\,]), so that Ji​j=(𝐣j)iJ_{ij}=(\mathbf{j}_{j})_{i}. Suppose that two columns, indexed by a,b∈{1,…,p}a,b\in\{1,\dots,p\} with a≠ba\neq b, satisfy the near-proportionality condition 𝐣b=c​𝐣a+𝛅\mathbf{j}_{b}=c\,\mathbf{j}_{a}+\boldsymbol{\delta} with c≠0c\neq 0, 𝛅∈ℝm\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, and ‖𝛅‖=O⁡(ε)\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|=O(\varepsilon), where ε>0\varepsilon>0 is the law-specific exponent gap. Define the m×2m\times 2 matrix formed by extracting these two columns from JJ:

J1≔[𝐣a∣𝐣b]∈ℝm×2,i.e.,​(J1)i​1=Ji​a,(J1)i​2=Ji​b,J_{1}\coloneqq[\,\mathbf{j}_{a}\mid\mathbf{j}_{b}\,]\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times 2},\hskip 18.49988pt\text{i.e.,}\hskip 9.24994pt(J_{1})_{i1}=J_{ia},\;\;(J_{1})_{i2}=J_{ib}, (20)

Since J1T​J1J_{1}^{T}J_{1} is a 2×22\times 2 real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix (symmetry: (J1T​J1)T=J1T​J1(J_{1}^{T}J_{1})^{T}=J_{1}^{T}J_{1}; positive semidefiniteness: 𝐯T​J1T​J1​𝐯=‖J1​𝐯‖2≥0\mathbf{v}^{T}J_{1}^{T}J_{1}\,\mathbf{v}=\|J_{1}\mathbf{v}\|^{2}\geq 0 for all 𝐯∈ℝ2\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}), the spectral theorem guarantees that it possesses an orthonormal eigenbasis. Let 𝐰∈ℝ2\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} be a unit eigenvector corresponding to its smallest eigenvalue:

(J1T​J1)​𝐰=λmin​(J1T​J1)​𝐰,‖𝐰‖=1.(J_{1}^{T}J_{1})\,\mathbf{w}=\lambda_{\min}(J_{1}^{T}J_{1})\,\mathbf{w},\hskip 18.49988pt\|\mathbf{w}\|=1. (21)

Construct the test vector 𝐰~∈ℝp\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} by placing the entries of 𝐰\mathbf{w} in positions aa and bb and zeros elsewhere:

w~j≔{w1if ​j=a,w2if ​j=b,0otherwise.\tilde{w}_{j}\coloneqq\begin{cases}w_{1}&\text{if }j=a,\\ w_{2}&\text{if }j=b,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (22)

Then ‖𝐰~‖=‖𝐰‖=1\|\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\|=\|\mathbf{w}\|=1 and:

λmin​(JT​J)≤𝐰~T​(JT​J)​𝐰~=λmin​(J1T​J1)=O⁡(ε2),\lambda_{\min}(J^{T}J)\leq\tilde{\mathbf{w}}^{T}(J^{T}J)\,\tilde{\mathbf{w}}=\lambda_{\min}(J_{1}^{T}J_{1})=O(\varepsilon^{2}), (23)

and consequently, under the global dominance assumption (Section 3.1),

κ⁡(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε−2)​with​λmax​(JT​J)=Θ⁡(1).\kappa(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2})\hskip 9.24994pt\text{with}\hskip 9.24994pt\lambda_{\max}(J^{T}J)=\Theta(1). (3)

We proceed in three steps: (i) show that Proposition 1’s assumption 𝐣b=c​𝐣a+𝜹\mathbf{j}_{b}=c\,\mathbf{j}_{a}+\boldsymbol{\delta} forces λmin​(J1T​J1)=O⁡(ε2)\lambda_{\min}(J_{1}^{T}J_{1})=O(\varepsilon^{2}); (ii) use the Rayleigh quotient to transfer this to the full p×pp\times p Gram matrix; (iii) conclude the condition-number bound.

Step 1: λmin​(J1T​J1)=O⁡(ε2)\lambda_{\min}(J_{1}^{T}J_{1})=O(\varepsilon^{2}).

By the near proportionality assumption of Proposition 1, 𝐣b=c​𝐣a+𝜹\mathbf{j}_{b}=c\,\mathbf{j}_{a}+\boldsymbol{\delta} with ‖𝜹‖=O⁡(ε)\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|=O(\varepsilon). The 2×22\times 2 Gram matrix of J1=[𝐣a∣𝐣b]J_{1}=[\,\mathbf{j}_{a}\mid\mathbf{j}_{b}\,] is:

G≔J1T​J1=(‖𝐣a‖2𝐣aT​𝐣b𝐣bT​𝐣a‖𝐣b‖2).G\coloneqq J_{1}^{T}J_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}\|\mathbf{j}_{a}\|^{2}&\mathbf{j}_{a}^{T}\mathbf{j}_{b}\\[3.0pt] \mathbf{j}_{b}^{T}\mathbf{j}_{a}&\|\mathbf{j}_{b}\|^{2}\end{pmatrix}. (24)

Substituting 𝐣b=c​𝐣a+𝜹\mathbf{j}_{b}=c\,\mathbf{j}_{a}+\boldsymbol{\delta}:

‖𝐣b‖2\displaystyle\|\mathbf{j}_{b}\|^{2} =c2​‖𝐣a‖2+2​c​𝐣aT​𝜹+‖𝜹‖2,\displaystyle=c^{2}\,\|\mathbf{j}_{a}\|^{2}+2c\,\mathbf{j}_{a}^{T}\boldsymbol{\delta}+\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|^{2}, (25)
𝐣aT​𝐣b\displaystyle\mathbf{j}_{a}^{T}\mathbf{j}_{b} =c​‖𝐣a‖2+𝐣aT​𝜹.\displaystyle=c\,\|\mathbf{j}_{a}\|^{2}+\mathbf{j}_{a}^{T}\boldsymbol{\delta}. (26)

Write s≔‖𝐣a‖2>0s\coloneqq\|\mathbf{j}_{a}\|^{2}>0 and η≔𝐣aT​𝜹\eta\coloneqq\mathbf{j}_{a}^{T}\boldsymbol{\delta} (so |η|≤‖𝐣a‖​‖𝜹‖=O⁡(ε)|\eta|\leq\|\mathbf{j}_{a}\|\,\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|=O(\varepsilon) by Cauchy-Schwarz). Then:

G=(sc​s+ηc​s+ηc2​s+2​c​η+‖𝜹‖2).G=\begin{pmatrix}s&cs+\eta\\[2.0pt] cs+\eta&c^{2}s+2c\eta+\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|^{2}\end{pmatrix}.

The determinant is:

det(G)\displaystyle\det(G) =s⁡(c2​s+2​c​η+‖𝜹‖2)−(c​s+η)2\displaystyle=s\,(c^{2}s+2c\eta+\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|^{2})-(cs+\eta)^{2}
=s​c2​s+2​s​c​η+s​‖𝜹‖2−c2​s2−2​c​s​η−η2\displaystyle=s\,c^{2}s+2sc\eta+s\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|^{2}-c^{2}s^{2}-2cs\eta-\eta^{2}
=s​‖𝜹‖2−η2.\displaystyle=s\,\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|^{2}-\eta^{2}. (27)

By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to 𝐣a\mathbf{j}_{a} and 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta}: η2=(𝐣aT​𝜹)2≤‖𝐣a‖2​‖𝜹‖2=s​‖𝜹‖2\eta^{2}=(\mathbf{j}_{a}^{T}\boldsymbol{\delta})^{2}\leq\|\mathbf{j}_{a}\|^{2}\,\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|^{2}=s\,\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|^{2}, with equality if and only if 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} is proportional to 𝐣a\mathbf{j}_{a} (which would make 𝐣b\mathbf{j}_{b} exactly proportional to 𝐣a\mathbf{j}_{a} and hence det(G)=0\det(G)=0). In general:

0≤det(G)=s​‖𝜹‖2−η2≤s​‖𝜹‖2=O⁡(ε2).0\;\leq\;\det(G)\;=\;s\,\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|^{2}-\eta^{2}\;\leq\;s\,\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|^{2}\;=\;O(\varepsilon^{2}). (28)

Since GG is a 2×22\times 2 positive semidefinite matrix with tr⁡(G)=s+c2​s+O⁡(ε)=Θ⁡(1)\operatorname{tr}(G)=s+c^{2}s+O(\varepsilon)=\Theta(1), its eigenvalues λ+≥λ−≥0\lambda_{+}\geq\lambda_{-}\geq 0 satisfy λ++λ−=tr⁡(G)=Θ⁡(1)\lambda_{+}+\lambda_{-}=\operatorname{tr}(G)=\Theta(1) and λ+⋅λ−=det(G)=O⁡(ε2)\lambda_{+}\cdot\lambda_{-}=\det(G)=O(\varepsilon^{2}). Therefore:

λ−​(G)=det(G)λ+​(G)=O⁡(ε2)Θ⁡(1)=O⁡(ε2).\lambda_{-}(G)=\frac{\det(G)}{\lambda_{+}(G)}=\frac{O(\varepsilon^{2})}{\Theta(1)}=O(\varepsilon^{2}). (29)

Let 𝐰∈ℝ2\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} be a unit eigenvector of GG corresponding to λ−=λmin​(G)\lambda_{-}=\lambda_{\min}(G), as defined in (21). Then:

𝐰T​G​𝐰=λmin​(G)=O⁡(ε2).\mathbf{w}^{T}G\,\mathbf{w}=\lambda_{\min}(G)=O(\varepsilon^{2}). (30)

Step 2: Rayleigh-quotient transfer to the full system.

Partition J=[J1∣J2]J=[\,J_{1}\mid J_{2}\,] where J1∈ℝm×2J_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times 2} consists of columns aa and bb, and J2∈ℝm×(p−2)J_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times(p-2)} contains all remaining columns. Construct the padded test vector 𝐰~∈ℝp\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} as in the proposition statement (w~a=w1\tilde{w}_{a}=w_{1}, w~b=w2\tilde{w}_{b}=w_{2}, w~j=0\tilde{w}_{j}=0 otherwise), so that ‖𝐰~‖=‖𝐰‖=1\|\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\|=\|\mathbf{w}\|=1.

The full Gram matrix has block structure:

JT​J=(J1T​J1J1T​J2J2T​J1J2T​J2).J^{T}J=\begin{pmatrix}J_{1}^{T}J_{1}&J_{1}^{T}J_{2}\\[2.0pt] J_{2}^{T}J_{1}&J_{2}^{T}J_{2}\end{pmatrix}. (31)

Evaluating the quadratic form at 𝐰~\tilde{\mathbf{w}}:

𝐰~T​(JT​J)​𝐰~\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{w}}^{T}(J^{T}J)\,\tilde{\mathbf{w}} =(𝐰𝟎)T​(J1T​J1J1T​J2J2T​J1J2T​J2)​(𝐰𝟎)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{w}\\ \mathbf{0}\end{pmatrix}^{\!T}\begin{pmatrix}J_{1}^{T}J_{1}&J_{1}^{T}J_{2}\\ J_{2}^{T}J_{1}&J_{2}^{T}J_{2}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{w}\\ \mathbf{0}\end{pmatrix}
=𝐰T​(J1T​J1)​𝐰+𝟎T​(J2T​J1)​𝐰⏟= 0+𝐰T​(J1T​J2)​ 0⏟= 0+𝟎T​(J2T​J2)​ 0⏟= 0\displaystyle=\mathbf{w}^{T}(J_{1}^{T}J_{1})\,\mathbf{w}+\underbrace{\mathbf{0}^{T}(J_{2}^{T}J_{1})\,\mathbf{w}}_{=\,0}+\underbrace{\mathbf{w}^{T}(J_{1}^{T}J_{2})\,\mathbf{0}}_{=\,0}+\underbrace{\mathbf{0}^{T}(J_{2}^{T}J_{2})\,\mathbf{0}}_{=\,0}
=𝐰T​(J1T​J1)​𝐰=λmin​(J1T​J1)=O⁡(ε2).\displaystyle=\mathbf{w}^{T}(J_{1}^{T}J_{1})\,\mathbf{w}=\lambda_{\min}(J_{1}^{T}J_{1})=O(\varepsilon^{2}). (32)

By the Rayleigh-Ritz principle, λmin​(M)=min‖𝐯‖=1⁡𝐯T​M​𝐯\lambda_{\min}(M)=\min_{\|\mathbf{v}\|=1}\mathbf{v}^{T}M\mathbf{v}, so every unit 𝐯\mathbf{v} satisfies λmin​(M)≤𝐯T​M​𝐯\lambda_{\min}(M)\leq\mathbf{v}^{T}M\mathbf{v}:

λmin​(JT​J)≤𝐰~T​(JT​J)​𝐰~=O⁡(ε2).\lambda_{\min}(J^{T}J)\leq\tilde{\mathbf{w}}^{T}(J^{T}J)\,\tilde{\mathbf{w}}=O(\varepsilon^{2}). (33)

Step 3: Condition-number bound.

For the upper bound on λmax\lambda_{\max}, note that λmax​(JT​J)\lambda_{\max}(J^{T}J) is at least λmax​(J1T​J1)≥tr⁡(G)/2=Θ⁡(1)\lambda_{\max}(J_{1}^{T}J_{1})\geq\operatorname{tr}(G)/2=\Theta(1) (since GG has two eigenvalues summing to tr⁡(G)=Θ⁡(1)\operatorname{tr}(G)=\Theta(1), the larger is at least half the trace). More generally, λmax​(JT​J)≤tr⁡(JT​J)=‖J‖F2=Θ⁡(1)\lambda_{\max}(J^{T}J)\leq\operatorname{tr}(J^{T}J)=\|J\|_{F}^{2}=\Theta(1) for any non-degenerate dataset (all columns of JJ have bounded norms). Therefore λmax​(JT​J)=Θ⁡(1)\lambda_{\max}(J^{T}J)=\Theta(1), and:

κ⁡(JT​J)=λmax​(JT​J)λmin​(JT​J)≥Θ⁡(1)O⁡(ε2)=Ω⁡(ε−2).\kappa(J^{T}J)=\frac{\lambda_{\max}(J^{T}J)}{\lambda_{\min}(J^{T}J)}\geq\frac{\Theta(1)}{O(\varepsilon^{2})}=\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2}). (34)

The matching upper bound κ⁡(JT​J)=O⁡(ε−2)\kappa(J^{T}J)=O(\varepsilon^{-2}) follows from the global dominance assumption (Section 3.1): since (A,B)(A,B) is the only source of small eigenvalues, λmin​(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε2)\lambda_{\min}(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{2}), yielding κ⁡(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε−2)\kappa(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}).∎

B.4 Appendix - Cauchy-Schwarz gap identity

Lemma 2 (Cauchy-Schwarz gap identity).

Let 𝐟,𝐠∈ℝm\mathbf{f},\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} with gi=c​fi​hig_{i}=c\,f_{i}\,h_{i} for a scalar c≠0c\neq 0 and arbitrary hi>0h_{i}>0. Define the power-law weights wi≔fi2/∑jfj2w_{i}\coloneqq f_{i}^{2}\!\big/\sum_{j}f_{j}^{2} and the weighted variance σw2​(h)≔∑iwi​hi2−(∑iwi​hi)2\sigma_{w}^{2}(h)\coloneqq\sum_{i}w_{i}\,h_{i}^{2}-\bigl(\sum_{i}w_{i}\,h_{i}\bigr)^{\!2}. Then:

det(𝐟T​𝐟𝐟T​𝐠𝐠T​𝐟𝐠T​𝐠)=c2​(∑ifi2)2​σw2​(h).\det\!\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{f}^{T}\mathbf{f}\!\!\!\!&\mathbf{f}^{T}\mathbf{g}\\ \mathbf{g}^{T}\mathbf{f}\!\!\!\!&\mathbf{g}^{T}\mathbf{g}\end{pmatrix}=c^{2}\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{i}f_{i}^{2}\Bigr)^{\!2}\;\sigma_{w}^{2}(h). (35)
Proof.

Expand: 𝐟T​𝐠=c​∑ifi2​hi\mathbf{f}^{T}\mathbf{g}=c\sum_{i}f_{i}^{2}h_{i}, 𝐠T​𝐠=c2​∑ifi2​hi2\mathbf{g}^{T}\mathbf{g}=c^{2}\sum_{i}f_{i}^{2}h_{i}^{2}, so det=(∑ifi2)(c2∑ifi2hi2)−c2(∑ifi2hi)2=c2(∑ifi2)2[∑iwihi2−(∑iwihi)2]\det=(\sum_{i}f_{i}^{2})(c^{2}\sum_{i}f_{i}^{2}h_{i}^{2})-c^{2}(\sum_{i}f_{i}^{2}h_{i})^{2}=c^{2}(\sum_{i}f_{i}^{2})^{2}[\sum_{i}w_{i}h_{i}^{2}-(\sum_{i}w_{i}h_{i})^{2}]. ∎

For hi=Niηh_{i}=N_{i}^{\eta} with |η||\eta| small, a Taylor expansion gives:

σw2​(Niη)=η2​σw2​(log⁡Ni)+O⁡(|η|3),\sigma_{w}^{2}(N_{i}^{\eta})=\eta^{2}\,\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N_{i})+O(|\eta|^{3}), (36)

For Chinchilla, take η=α−β\eta=\alpha-\beta and ε≔|α−β|\varepsilon\coloneqq|\alpha-\beta| (Definition 3), so η2=ε2\eta^{2}=\varepsilon^{2}. Thus the same bound applies to hi=Niα−βh_{i}=N_{i}^{\alpha-\beta}, yielding a non-asymptotic condition-number bound depending on ε\varepsilon, the sample size nn, and the spread of {Ni}\{N_{i}\}.

B.5 Appendix - Chinchilla scaling law: detailed analysis

The Chinchilla parameter vector is 𝜽=[A,B,E,α,β]T\boldsymbol{\theta}=[A,B,E,\alpha,\beta]^{T} (p=5p=5). The following analysis holds on a single collinear ray Di=kℓ​NiD_{i}=k_{\ell}N_{i} (i.e., K=1K=1 or a single fixed ratio kℓk_{\ell} from the design); the scale-coefficient columns then satisfy:

∂L^i∂B=kℓ−β⏟c​Ni−α​Niα−β,\frac{\partial\hat{L}_{i}}{\partial B}=\underbrace{k_{\ell}^{-\beta}}_{c}\,N_{i}^{-\alpha}\,N_{i}^{\alpha-\beta}, (37)

with ε≔|α−β|\varepsilon\coloneqq|\alpha-\beta|. The corresponding residual Jacobian entries are Ji​A=−∂L^i/∂AJ_{iA}=-\partial\hat{L}_{i}/\partial A and Ji​B=−∂L^i/∂BJ_{iB}=-\partial\hat{L}_{i}/\partial B, but (JT​J)A,B(J^{T}J)_{A,B} equals the Gram matrix of (∂L^/∂A,∂L^/∂B)(\partial\hat{L}/\partial A,\,\partial\hat{L}/\partial B) because both columns pick up the same sign. The determinant of the (A,B)(A,B) sub-block of JT​JJ^{T}J satisfies:

det((JT​J)A,B)=O⁡(ε2),\det\!\left((J^{T}J)_{A,B}\right)=O(\varepsilon^{2}), (38)

so κ⁡((JT​J)A,B)=Θ⁡(ε−2)\kappa((J^{T}J)_{A,B})=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}). Applying Proposition 1 (under the (A,B)(A,B)-dominance assumption of Section 3.1), κ⁡(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε−2)\kappa(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}) for the full 5×55\times 5 system. For the empirical gap |α−β|≈0.06|\alpha-\beta|\approx 0.06, the condition number is on the order of 10210^{2}-10310^{3}.

Explicit finite-sample bound. This subsection provides the explicit finite-sample bound for the Chinchilla law (1) on a single collinear ray (K=1K=1, Di=kℓ​NiD_{i}=k_{\ell}N_{i} for a fixed ratio kℓk_{\ell}).

Applying Lemma 2 with fi=Ni−αf_{i}=N_{i}^{-\alpha}, c=kℓ−βc=k_{\ell}^{-\beta}, and hi=Niα−βh_{i}=N_{i}^{\alpha-\beta}, the sub-block determinant admits the exact factorisation:

det((JT​J)A,B)=kℓ−2​β​Φ2 2​σw2​(Niα−β),\det\!\left((J^{T}J)_{A,B}\right)=k_{\ell}^{-2\beta}\,\Phi_{2}^{\,2}\;\sigma_{w}^{2}\!\bigl(N_{i}^{\alpha-\beta}\bigr), (39)

where Φ2≔∑i=1nNi−2​α\Phi_{2}\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}N_{i}^{-2\alpha} and the weights are wi=Ni−2​α/Φ2w_{i}=N_{i}^{-2\alpha}/\Phi_{2}. Using the Taylor expansion (36):

det((JT​J)A,B)≈kℓ−2​β​Φ2 2​ε2​σw2​(log⁡N),\det\!\left((J^{T}J)_{A,B}\right)\approx k_{\ell}^{-2\beta}\,\Phi_{2}^{\,2}\;\varepsilon^{2}\;\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N), (40)

with σw2​(log⁡N)=∑iwi​(log⁡Ni)2−(∑iwi​log⁡Ni)2\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N)=\sum_{i}w_{i}(\log N_{i})^{2}-\bigl(\sum_{i}w_{i}\log N_{i}\bigr)^{\!2}. The condition number of the sub-block is therefore:

κ⁡((JT​J)A,B)≈tr⁡((JT​J)A,B)2kℓ−2​β​Φ2 2​ε2​σw2​(log⁡N),\kappa\bigl((J^{T}J)_{A,B}\bigr)\approx\frac{\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl((J^{T}J)_{A,B}\bigr)^{2}}{k_{\ell}^{-2\beta}\,\Phi_{2}^{\,2}\;\varepsilon^{2}\;\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N)}\,, (41)

which makes the three sources of ill-conditioning explicit: (i) small exponent gap ε→0\varepsilon\to 0; (ii) narrow model-size range, i.e. small σw2​(log⁡N)\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N) when the NiN_{i} are clustered; and (iii) finite sample effects through Φ2\Phi_{2} and the weights wiw_{i}, which concentrate on the smallest models and reduce the effective sample diversity. For the empirical gap |α−β|≈0.06|\alpha-\beta|\approx 0.06, equation (41) yields a condition number on the order of 10210^{2}-10310^{3}, rendering the system numerically ill-conditioned.∎

B.6 Appendix - Full Jacobian and tight conditioning

Full Jacobian analysis. The preceding argument concerns only the AA and BB columns. We now list the five model sensitivities ∂L^i/∂θj\partial\hat{L}_{i}/\partial\theta_{j} on a single collinear ray Di=kℓ​NiD_{i}=k_{\ell}N_{i}; by (10), the residual Jacobian JJ is obtained by negating each of these columns, so JT​JJ^{T}J equals the Gram matrix of the sensitivities below. We claim the (E,α,β)(E,\alpha,\beta) coordinates do not rescue the conditioning. The complete set of partial derivatives is:

∂L^i∂A\displaystyle\frac{\partial\hat{L}_{i}}{\partial A} =Ni−α,\displaystyle=N_{i}^{-\alpha}, ∂L^i∂B\displaystyle\hskip 18.49988pt\frac{\partial\hat{L}_{i}}{\partial B} =kℓ−β​Ni−β,\displaystyle=k_{\ell}^{-\beta}\,N_{i}^{-\beta},
∂L^i∂E\displaystyle\frac{\partial\hat{L}_{i}}{\partial E} =1,\displaystyle=1, ∂L^i∂α\displaystyle\hskip 18.49988pt\frac{\partial\hat{L}_{i}}{\partial\alpha} =−A​Ni−α​log⁡Ni,\displaystyle=-A\,N_{i}^{-\alpha}\log N_{i},
∂L^i∂β\displaystyle\frac{\partial\hat{L}_{i}}{\partial\beta} =−B​kℓ−β​Ni−β​(log⁡kℓ+log⁡Ni).\displaystyle=-B\,k_{\ell}^{-\beta}\,N_{i}^{-\beta}(\log k_{\ell}+\log N_{i}). (42)

Observe that (writing 𝐣u\mathbf{j}_{u} for the mm-vector with entries ∂L^i/∂u\partial\hat{L}_{i}/\partial u) 𝐣α=−A​diag⁡(log⁡Ni)​𝐣A\mathbf{j}_{\alpha}=-A\,\operatorname{diag}(\log N_{i})\,\mathbf{j}_{A} and 𝐣β=−B⁡(log⁡kℓ)​𝐣B−B​diag⁡(log⁡Ni)​𝐣B\mathbf{j}_{\beta}=-B\,(\log k_{\ell})\,\mathbf{j}_{B}-B\,\operatorname{diag}(\log N_{i})\,\mathbf{j}_{B}. Using 𝐣B≈c​𝐣A+O⁡(ε)\mathbf{j}_{B}\approx c\,\mathbf{j}_{A}+O(\varepsilon) (from (37)), both exponent columns lie approximately in the two-dimensional subspace span⁡{𝐣A,diag⁡(log⁡Ni)​𝐣A}\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{j}_{A},\,\operatorname{diag}(\log N_{i})\,\mathbf{j}_{A}\}. In particular, if 𝐣B=c​𝐣A\mathbf{j}_{B}=c\,\mathbf{j}_{A} exactly, then 𝐣β−(B​c/A)​𝐣α=−B​c​(log⁡kℓ)​𝐣A\mathbf{j}_{\beta}-(Bc/A)\,\mathbf{j}_{\alpha}=-Bc(\log k_{\ell})\,\mathbf{j}_{A}, so 𝐣α\mathbf{j}_{\alpha} and 𝐣β\mathbf{j}_{\beta} are not scalar multiples whenever log⁡kℓ≠0\log k_{\ell}\neq 0; more generally they share the same underlying column space as the scale-coefficient pair and therefore do not contribute an independent direction that overlaps the near-null space of (JT​J)A,B(J^{T}J)_{A,B}. The EE-column of sensitivities is 𝟏\mathbf{1}, hence the EE-column of JJ is −𝟏-\mathbf{1}; either way it is linearly independent of the power-law columns but likewise does not break the collinearity between the AA/BB pair.

By Proposition 1, the near-null eigenvector 𝐰\mathbf{w} of (JT​J)A,B(J^{T}J)_{A,B}, extended to 𝐰~∈ℝ5\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\in\mathbb{R}^{5} with zeros in the (E,α,β)(E,\alpha,\beta) coordinates matching (22), satisfies 𝐰~T​(JT​J)​𝐰~=O⁡(ε2)\tilde{\mathbf{w}}^{T}(J^{T}J)\,\tilde{\mathbf{w}}=O(\varepsilon^{2}), hence κ⁡(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε−2)\kappa(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}) for the full 5×55\times 5 system under the dominance assumption in Section 3.1.∎

B.7 Appendix - Repeated-data scaling law: detailed analysis

This subsection analyses the Jacobian of the repeated-data law on a single collinear ray (K=1K=1, Di=kℓ​NiD_{i}=k_{\ell}N_{i}). muennighoff2023scaling retain the Chinchilla form but replace NN and DD with effective quantities N′N^{\prime} and D′D^{\prime} that decay under repetition:

with D′=UD+UDRD∗(1−e−RD/RD∗)D^{\prime}=U_{D}+U_{D}R_{D}^{*}(1-e^{-R_{D}/R_{D}^{*}}), UD=min⁡{DC,D}U_{D}=\min\{D_{C},D\}, RD=(D/UD)−1R_{D}=(D/U_{D})-1, and analogously N′=UN+UNRN∗(1−e−RN/RN∗)N^{\prime}=U_{N}+U_{N}R_{N}^{*}(1-e^{-R_{N}/R_{N}^{*}}), RN=(N/UN)−1R_{N}=(N/U_{N})-1, with UNU_{N} Chinchilla-optimal for UDU_{D}. When RD=RN=0R_{D}=R_{N}=0 (single epoch, no excess parameters), D′=DD^{\prime}=D and N′=NN^{\prime}=N, recovering Chinchilla exactly.

Under Di=kℓ​NiD_{i}=k_{\ell}N_{i}, both Di′D_{i}^{\prime} and Ni′N_{i}^{\prime} become deterministic functions of NiN_{i}; write Di′=ϕ⁡(Ni)D_{i}^{\prime}=\phi(N_{i}) and Ni′=ψ⁡(Ni)N_{i}^{\prime}=\psi(N_{i}). The scale-coefficient sensitivities are ∂L^i/∂A=ψ​(Ni)−α\partial\hat{L}_{i}/\partial A=\psi(N_{i})^{-\alpha} and ∂L^i/∂B=ϕ​(Ni)−β\partial\hat{L}_{i}/\partial B=\phi(N_{i})^{-\beta}, so Lemma 2 applies to the scale-coefficient pair with fi=ψ​(Ni)−αf_{i}=\psi(N_{i})^{-\alpha}, c=kℓ−βc=k_{\ell}^{-\beta}, and hi=kℓβ​ϕ​(Ni)−β​ψ​(Ni)αh_{i}=k_{\ell}^{\beta}\,\phi(N_{i})^{-\beta}\,\psi(N_{i})^{\alpha}, yielding det((JT​J)A,B)=c2​Φ2 2​σw2​(h)\det\!\left((J^{T}J)_{A,B}\right)=c^{2}\,\Phi_{2}^{\,2}\,\sigma_{w}^{2}(h) with Φ2=∑iψ​(Ni)−2​α\Phi_{2}=\sum_{i}\psi(N_{i})^{-2\alpha} and wi=ψ​(Ni)−2​α/Φ2w_{i}=\psi(N_{i})^{-2\alpha}/\Phi_{2}. The conditioning of the (A,B)(A,B) sub-block therefore depends on the variance of hih_{i} across the ray, which differs sharply between two regimes.

Unsaturated regime (RD=RN=0R_{D}=R_{N}=0). Here ϕ⁡(N)=kℓ​N\phi(N)=k_{\ell}N and ψ⁡(N)=N\psi(N)=N, so hi=Niα−βh_{i}=N_{i}^{\alpha-\beta}. The Taylor expansion σw2​(Niα−β)≈ε2​σw2​(log⁡Ni)\sigma_{w}^{2}(N_{i}^{\,\alpha-\beta})\approx\varepsilon^{2}\,\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N_{i}) (with ε=|α−β|\varepsilon=|\alpha-\beta|) gives det((JT​J)A,B)=O⁡(ε2)\det((J^{T}J)_{A,B})=O(\varepsilon^{2}), so under the (A,B)(A,B)-dominance assumption of Section 3.1, κ⁡(JT​J)=Θ⁡(ε−2)\kappa(J^{T}J)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}) for the full 5×55\times 5 system - the law inherits Chinchilla’s ill-conditioning verbatim.

Saturated regime (RD,RN≠0R_{D},R_{N}\neq 0). Once the ratio ϕ⁡(Ni)/ψ⁡(Ni)\phi(N_{i})/\psi(N_{i}) varies systematically with NiN_{i}, hih_{i} ceases to be a pure power of NiN_{i}: the saturation curves of ϕ\phi and ψ\psi inject an ε\varepsilon-independent contribution into log⁡hi\log h_{i}. Concretely, σw2​(h)=Ω⁡(1)\sigma_{w}^{2}(h)=\Omega(1) as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, so the Taylor expansion that produced the ε2\varepsilon^{2} factor no longer applies. The scale-coefficient columns are no longer near-proportional, det((JT​J)A,B)=Ω⁡(1)\det((J^{T}J)_{A,B})=\Omega(1), and the design is generically well-conditioned with κ⁡(JT​J)=Θ⁡(1)\kappa(J^{T}J)=\Theta(1) - the saturation curvature itself breaks the degeneracy.

The repeated-data law therefore inherits the Θ⁡(ε−2)\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}) collinearity of Chinchilla only in the unsaturated regime. The (A,B)(A,B) sub-block of QQ is identically zero (as for Chinchilla) because L^\hat{L} is linear in AA and BB. Empirically, in our seed-paired comparisons the repeated-data law tracks the Chinchilla pattern (CO holdout R2R^{2} degrades and NC consistently wins), consistent with our multi-epoch fits sitting close to the unsaturated regime; we flag the saturated regime as a setting in which the formal guarantee does not apply.∎

B.10 Appendix - Identified submodels on a single collinear ray (K=1K=1)

This subsection provides the formal statements supporting Section 3.1. Throughout, we fix K=1K=1, i.e. all training points share a single TPP ratio kℓk_{\ell}, so Di=kℓ​NiD_{i}=k_{\ell}N_{i}. The reduced model L⁡(N)=ψ​N−α+EL(N)=\psi\,N^{-\alpha}+E with ψ≔A+B​kℓ−α\psi\coloneqq A+B\,k_{\ell}^{-\alpha} (equation (2)) is defined in the main text. We next define the power sums Φq\Phi_{q}, weights wiw_{i}, and σw2​(log⁡N)\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N) (Definitions 5, 6, and 7). Proposition 4 shows that the (ψ,α)(\psi,\alpha) Gram block of the reduced Jacobian has determinant ψ2​Φ2 2​σw2​(log⁡N)\psi^{2}\Phi_{2}^{\,2}\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N) (via Lemma 2 in Appendix B.4), positive for any design with at least two distinct model sizes and independent of ε\varepsilon, and Corollary 2 records an Θ⁡(ε−2)\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}) condition-number gain relative to the full model.

Let N1<⋯<NnN_{1}<\cdots<N_{n} be the distinct model sizes (as in the observation model, Section 3).

Definition 5 (Power sums).

For q>0q>0, the power sums are Φq≔∑i=1nNi−q​α\Phi_{q}\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}N_{i}^{-q\alpha}. In particular, Φ2≔∑i=1nNi−2​α\Phi_{2}\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}N_{i}^{-2\alpha}.

Definition 6 (Weights).

Given Φ2\Phi_{2} from Definition 5, the weights are wi≔Ni−2​α/Φ2w_{i}\coloneqq N_{i}^{-2\alpha}/\Phi_{2} for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n.

Definition 7 (Weighted log-variance).

Given weights (wi)(w_{i}) from Definition 6, the weighted log-variance is σw2​(log⁡N)≔∑i=1nwi​(log⁡Ni)2−(∑i=1nwi​log⁡Ni)2\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N)\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}(\log N_{i})^{2}-\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\log N_{i}\bigr)^{\!2}.

Proposition 4 (Identification of the reduced model).

The Gram determinant of the (ψ,α)(\psi,\alpha) sub-block of JredT​JredJ_{\mathrm{red}}^{T}J_{\mathrm{red}} is

det((JredT​Jred)ψ,α)=ψ2​Φ2 2​σw2​(log⁡N),\det\!\bigl((J_{\mathrm{red}}^{T}J_{\mathrm{red}})_{\psi,\alpha}\bigr)=\psi^{2}\,\Phi_{2}^{\,2}\;\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N), (53)

where σw2​(log⁡N)\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N) is as in Definition 7. The determinant is positive for any design with at least two distinct model sizes and is independent of the exponent gap ε\varepsilon. The full 3×33\times 3 matrix JredT​JredJ_{\mathrm{red}}^{T}J_{\mathrm{red}} is non-singular.

Corollary 2 (Condition-number improvement).

In the setting of Proposition 4, κfull/κred=Θ⁡(ε−2)\kappa_{\mathrm{full}}/\kappa_{\mathrm{red}}=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}). For |α−β|≈0.06|\alpha-\beta|\approx 0.06, this is a factor of 10210^{2}-10310^{3}.

B.10.1 Identified submodels: proofs

Proof of Proposition 4.

Apply Lemma 2 with fi=Ni−αf_{i}=N_{i}^{-\alpha} (the ψ\psi-sensitivity ∂L^i/∂ψ\partial\hat{L}_{i}/\partial\psi), gi=c​fi​hig_{i}=c\,f_{i}\,h_{i} where c=−ψc=-\psi and hi=log⁡Nih_{i}=\log N_{i} (so that gi=∂L^i/∂αg_{i}=\partial\hat{L}_{i}/\partial\alpha). The Gram determinant is c2​(∑fi2)2​σw2​(h)=ψ2​Φ2 2​σw2​(log⁡N)c^{2}\,(\sum f_{i}^{2})^{2}\,\sigma_{w}^{2}(h)=\psi^{2}\,\Phi_{2}^{\,2}\,\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N). No ε\varepsilon appears because the reduced model contains a single power-law term. ∎

Proof of Corollary 2.

From equation (40), the sub-block determinant of the full model scales as ε2​σw2​(log⁡N)\varepsilon^{2}\,\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N), while from equation (53) the corresponding determinant of the reduced model is proportional to σw2​(log⁡N)\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N) alone. The σw2​(log⁡N)\sigma_{w}^{2}(\log N) factors cancel in the ratio, leaving a factor of ε−2\varepsilon^{-2}. ∎

B.12 Appendix - Proof of Proposition 2 (TPP diversity and full-matrix conditioning)

We give a self-contained proof. Throughout, βeff\beta_{\mathrm{eff}} denotes the law-specific data-size exponent (Table 8). For any K≥1K\geq 1 distinct TPP ratios k1<⋯<kKk_{1}<\cdots<k_{K}, let each ratio contribute nℓ≥1n_{\ell}\geq 1 observations at model sizes {Ni}\{N_{i}\} (the same set for each ray, without loss of generality for the leading-order analysis). The training Jacobian is evaluated at the collinear design Di​ℓ=kℓ​NiD_{i\ell}=k_{\ell}N_{i}.

For any of the four scaling laws in Definition 3, the two scale-coefficient columns of JJ on observation (Ni,kℓ​Ni)(N_{i},k_{\ell}N_{i}) are (cf. Appendix B.5, eqn. (37) for Chinchilla; analogous expressions hold for the other three laws with the substitutions of Table 8):

(jA)i​ℓ=Ni−α,(jB)i​ℓ=kℓ−βeff​Ni−α​Niε~,(j_{A})_{i\ell}=N_{i}^{-\alpha},\hskip 18.49988pt(j_{B})_{i\ell}=k_{\ell}^{-\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}}\,N_{i}^{-\alpha}\,N_{i}^{\tilde{\varepsilon}}, (62)

where ε~\tilde{\varepsilon} is the signed native gap in each law (e.g. α−β\alpha-\beta for Chinchilla and repeated-data, αN−αD\alpha_{N}-\alpha_{D} for Kaplan, γN−γD\gamma_{N}-\gamma_{D} for Droppo-Elibol), so |ε~|=ε|\tilde{\varepsilon}|=\varepsilon in Definition 3, and the displayed α\alpha is the model-side exponent paired with βeff\beta_{\mathrm{eff}} as in Table 8.

The four entries of the 2×22\times 2 Gram sub-block GA,B=JA,BT​JA,BG_{A,B}=J_{A,B}^{T}J_{A,B} are obtained by summing over all m=n​Km=nK observations. Working at leading order in ε\varepsilon (i.e., Niε~=1+O⁡(ε)N_{i}^{\tilde{\varepsilon}}=1+O(\varepsilon), Ni2​ε~=1+O⁡(ε)N_{i}^{2\tilde{\varepsilon}}=1+O(\varepsilon)):

(GA,B)11\displaystyle(G_{A,B})_{11} =∑ℓ=1K∑i=1nNi−2​α=K​Φ2,\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{n}N_{i}^{-2\alpha}=K\,\Phi_{2}, (63)
